claims.text: An actively learned machine-learning potential combined with on-the-fly ab initio corrections will substantially reduce the cost of computing fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The hybrid method will maintain fidelity comparable to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
Training on configurations from both solid and liquid phases will provide a potential suitable for evaluating fusion properties.
Periodic reweighting or free-energy perturbation can explicitly account for electron–vibration coupling and anharmonic vibrational entropy.
The hybrid MLP approach can replace full AIMD for the proposed free-energy calculations.
The approach is applicable from just below to above the melting point.
The approach can be extended from elemental and binary systems to multicomponent high-entropy systems.
Periodic ab initio recalibration will retain the structural and vibrational features governing free-energy differences between solid and liquid phases.
The MLP will sample phase space more rapidly and at lower cost than AIMD.
Targeted ab initio corrections will preserve the accuracy of vibrational and electron–vibration interactions.
The hybrid strategy will preserve subtle entropy and anharmonic contributions needed to describe fusion.
The method will reduce computational time by approximately one order of magnitude relative to explicit AIMD.
Predicted phase-transition free energies, melting temperatures, and entropy contributions will remain within the uncertainty bounds of TOR-TILD and ab initio methods.
Explicit AIMD and TOR-TILD provide high-fidelity thermodynamic evaluations.
Explicit AIMD and TOR-TILD are computationally expensive, particularly for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
Adequate training-set coverage of both solid and liquid configurations is a condition for the method to work.
The method's applicability may diminish in systems with extreme electronic complexity or critical long-range correlations.
Transfer to multicomponent systems may require an exponential increase in ab initio reference data.
